title: Level 2 – International Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Becoming a Professional Nurse
intro: Professionalism in Nursing Practice Program Outline Welcome to GNPS Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse. Nurses entering an international healthcare system must adapt to different legislation, professional standards, regulatory expectations, delegation models and cultural contexts while maintaining safe and ethical care. This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations. It strengthens ethical reasoning, accountability, advocacy, documentation, interprofessional communication, cultural safety and safe adaptation to unfamiliar legal and organisational systems. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Interpret local nursing standards and codes of conduct Distinguish legal, ethical and professional responsibilities Apply informed consent, privacy and mandatory-reporting requirements Delegate and supervise according to scope and patient stability Use structured ethical decision-making in complex cases Advocate for patients across cultural and communication barriers Manage conflict and communicate assertively Document complex care and escalation clearly Seek guidance and consultation when limits are reached International practice requires more than transferring previous habits into a new country. The safe nurse understands the local regulatory framework, asks when uncertain and recognises that professional accountability remains personal even within a team. By completing Level 2, you should be able to provide ethically sound, culturally safe and legally responsible nursing care within international healthcare environments.

sections.title: Applying International Standards and Regulatory Requirements

content.text: Professional regulation differs between countries, but the underlying expectations are consistent: practise safely, maintain competence, protect the public and comply with lawful standards. An IQN must understand the local framework before practising independently.
Learning outcomes
Relate local regulation to professional nursing practice Interpret codes, standards and organisational policy
Adapt safely to unfamiliar legal systems Recognise when to seek advice
Regulatory Frameworks Nurse practice laws, registration conditions and professional standards define expectations for competence, conduct and accountability.
Codes and Standards Codes describe professional behaviour, while standards describe expected practice. Organisational policies provide local processes but do not replace professional judgement.
Mandatory Reporting Requirements may include reporting suspected abuse, impaired practice, serious misconduct or communicable disease. Nurses must know local obligations.
Safe Adaptation IQNs should complete orientation, verify scope and ask for supervision when systems or requirements are unfamiliar.

An IQN is uncertain whether a suspected safeguarding concern must be reported directly to an external authority. The nurse consults the local policy and senior clinician immediately rather than relying on previous-country practice.
Key learning points
Know the laws and standards that apply locally Policy supports but does not replace judgement
Understand mandatory-reporting duties Seeking clarification is professional practice

sections.title: Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making

content.text: Complex decisions arise when capacity is uncertain, family views conflict, treatment burdens are high or urgent action is required. Nurses need a transparent process that separates facts, values, law and professional obligations.
Learning outcomes
Assess factors affecting decision-making capacity Apply a structured ethical decision process
Support substitute or supported decision-making appropriately Escalate unresolved ethical conflict
Capacity is decision-specific and may fluctuate. It involves understanding, retaining, weighing information and communicating a choice.
Ethical Decision Framework A structured approach identifies the problem, gathers facts, clarifies stakeholders and values, reviews law and policy, considers options and documents the reasoning.

Supported and Substitute Decisions People should receive support to decide wherever possible. When lawful substitutes are required, decisions should reflect the person's known wishes, values and best interests.
Ethics Consultation Complex or unresolved conflict may require senior review, legal advice, ethics consultation or specialist support.

An older patient with fluctuating delirium refuses a procedure. The nurse identifies that capacity may vary, seeks urgent medical assessment, supports communication and ensures that any decision follows the legal process rather than assuming incapacity.
Key learning points
Capacity is specific and may change Support decision-making before replacing it
Use a transparent ethical framework Document the reasoning and consultation

International teams may include different nursing categories and support roles. Safe delegation requires knowledge of local scopes, patient stability and the competence of the person receiving the task. Advocacy is required when systems or decisions threaten patient rights.
Learning outcomes
Delegate according to local scope and competence Supervise and evaluate delegated care
Advocate during unsafe or discriminatory practice Communicate conflict assertively
Local Scope and Role Clarity Titles and responsibilities differ across systems. Nurses should verify role boundaries rather than assuming equivalence.
Supervision The delegating nurse provides direction, monitoring and follow-up proportionate to patient risk and worker competence.
Advocacy includes clarifying information, protecting vulnerable people, challenging unsafe orders and helping patients navigate the system.
Professional Disagreement Structured communication, evidence and escalation pathways help resolve disagreement without personal attack.

A nurse is asked to delegate a complex assessment to a worker whose role does not include clinical judgement. The nurse declines, explains the scope concern and proposes an appropriate alternative while ensuring the patient is assessed promptly.
Key learning points
Know the local scope of every team role Match delegation to patient stability and competence
Advocacy may require respectful challenge Escalate unresolved safety concerns

sections.title: Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication

content.text: International nurses care for people with diverse languages, values and experiences. Professionalism requires culturally safe communication, protection of information and awareness that power differences can affect participation.
Learning outcomes
Provide culturally safe professional care Use interpreters appropriately
Protect digital and verbal confidentiality Communicate across teams and cultures
Cultural Safety Cultural safety requires self-awareness, respectful enquiry and attention to how the patient experiences care. Nurses should ask rather than assume.

Communication Access Professional interpreters should be used for complex or high-risk discussions. Family members may support but should not replace qualified interpretation when accuracy or confidentiality matters.
Digital Privacy Electronic records, email, messaging and remote care require secure access and appropriate information sharing.
Interprofessional Communication Structured handover and closed-loop communication make responsibility and risk visible across disciplines.

A patient with limited English is asked to sign a consent form using a relative as interpreter. The nurse pauses the process, arranges a professional interpreter and ensures the patient receives a clear explanation before deciding.
Key learning points
Cultural respect does not reduce safety standards Use professional interpreters for complex information
Protect confidentiality in every medium Make responsibility clear during handover

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 9 - Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to apply international standards, reason through complex ethical issues, delegate safely, advocate effectively and provide culturally safe professional care. You are now prepared for Level 3, where the focus moves to ethical leadership, governance and global professional integrity.
